summary: Delete all duplicates from a sorted linked list so each value appears once.
mainInsight: Duplicates are adjacent in a sorted list, so for each node skip forward past all nodes with the same value and relink once.

approaches.name: Single pass skipping equal nodes
approaches.summary: curr.next = first node with a different value.

approaches.name: Hash set
weaknesses: Unneeded because the list is sorted

promptVariants: Which technique solves this problem, and what in the statement or constraints points to it?
Name the technique you would use here and the clue in the problem that tells you.
What approach fits this problem, and which part of the statement gives it away?
cards.answer: Single pass skipping nodes with an equal value, relinking once per run. Clue: The list is sorted, so duplicates are adjacent and can be removed by comparing each node with the next one.
keyPoints: The list is sorted, so duplicates are adjacent and can be removed by comparing each node with the next one.
cards.explanation: Sorting groups equal values together, so a node only has to be compared with its neighbour.

promptVariants: What property makes in-place deduplication easy?
Why don't you need a hash set?
options: The list is sorted, so duplicates are adjacent
The list is doubly linked, so any node is reachable
The values are positive, so sums never drop
The list has a sentinel node marking the end of it
cards.answer: The list is sorted, so duplicates are adjacent
cards.explanation: Comparing neighbours is enough to detect duplicates.

promptVariants: What does the inner `while tmp and tmp.val == curr.val` loop do?
Explain how the links are rewritten.
cards.answer: It advances tmp to the first node whose value differs from curr's; then curr.next = tmp unlinks the whole run of duplicates in one assignment and curr moves to tmp.
keyPoints: Unlink the run in one step
cards.explanation: Each node is visited once overall.

promptVariants: Is a dummy node needed here?
Why can the head never be removed?
options: No: the first node of each value is kept, so the head stays
Yes, otherwise the head node is lost when it is removed
Only when the head value itself is a duplicate of the next
Only for empty lists and for lists with a single node
cards.answer: No: the first node of each value is kept, so the head stays
cards.explanation: Only later duplicates are deleted, so head remains valid (an empty list is handled by the initial check).
